items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Your core temperature varies by less than 1 degree all day
items.claim: Air temperature swings by 30 degrees C between Australian outback day and night. Sahara desert: 50 C day, 0 C night. Yet healthy human core temperature stays at 36.5-37.5 C across these extremes. We are walking thermostats.
items.prompt: How does the body hold core temperature constant?

options.text: The skin acts as insulation only

Negative feedback through the hypothalamus: sensors monitor core temperature; effectors include sweating (cooling), vasodilation/vasoconstriction (heat dump or retention), shivering (heat production), and behavioural responses (seek shade, put on clothes)
Body heat is generated constantly at the same rate

items.reveal:
The preoptic area of the hypothalamus contains warm-sensitive and cold-sensitive neurons. They integrate skin temperature (peripheral) and blood temperature (core) and adjust effector outputs.

When too hot: blood vessels in skin dilate; sweat glands release ~0.5-1.5 L/hour (up to 3 L/hour in heat-acclimated athletes); behaviour (seek shade).

When too cold: skin vessels constrict; shivering (involuntary skeletal muscle activity, heat output up to 5x resting); brown fat thermogenesis (less in adults); piloerection (goose bumps — useless on hairless humans but works in furred mammals); behaviour (seek shelter).

Fever is a deliberately raised set-point — the hypothalamus is told (by pyrogens) that 38.5 C is the new target. Your body now defends 38.5 the way it usually defends 37.

Heatstroke: thermoregulation fails at core temperatures above ~40 C. Mortality rises rapidly. Conversely, deep hypothermia (<30 C) shuts down cardiac function — but has been used surgically to extend safe ischemia times.

The set-point isn't constant: circadian variation (~0.5 C lower at night), menstrual cycle (~0.3 C higher post-ovulation), age-related decline in regulation precision.
items.why: Homeostasis is usually drawn as a circle on a board. It's an integration of dozens of mechanisms across the whole body — and breaks down in fascinating ways (fever, heatstroke, hypothermia) when stressed.

items.title: A woman who died in 1951 still has dividing cells today
items.claim: Normal human cells divide about 50 times and then stop (the Hayflick limit). HeLa cells, taken from Henrietta Lacks's cervical tumour in 1951, divide indefinitely. They are in laboratories on every continent.

options.text: Constitutive expression of telomerase — the enzyme that rebuilds telomeres on chromosome ends — allows them to divide without losing telomeric DNA, bypassing the Hayflick limit. The HPV-derived oncogenes E6 and E7 also disable normal tumour suppressors
Special preservation chemicals keep them alive
All cancer cells are technically immortal

items.reveal_title: Telomeres, telomerase, and the loophole around cell senescence
items.reveal:
Linear chromosomes lose a small amount of DNA from their ends with each replication (the 'end replication problem'). Once telomeres reach a critical short length, cells trigger senescence — the Hayflick limit, named after Leonard Hayflick (1961).

Most adult cells suppress telomerase. Germline cells, stem cells and most cancers reactivate it. HeLa cells express telomerase robustly. Combined with disabled tumour suppressors (p53 and Rb, neutralised by HPV-18 oncoproteins), they grow without limit.

HeLa cells were the first immortal human cell line. They were taken without Henrietta Lacks's consent. The ethical legacy is still being addressed — her family didn't learn the cells existed until 1973, and only signed an agreement with the NIH on access to her genome in 2013.
items.why: Cell death is taught as inevitable. The cellular machinery to bypass it exists; cancer cells exploit it; HeLa cells made it visible.
